campaign.name: Youth Camp | Parents
campaign.objective: Fill 30 Youth Camp places with players aged 11 to 15 before registration closes on 23 September.

concepts.name: Kids Use What Works
concepts.strategy: Start with the sensible choices young players make in games, then show why training creates room to develop the parts that are not ready yet.
concepts.audience: Parents of basketball players aged 11 to 15 who want their child to add to a game that already has dependable strengths.
concepts.proposition: A full day of coaching, repetition and live basketball where players can try, correct and use new skills.

ads.primary_text:
If your kid can get to the basket going right, they’re going to keep going right.

Of course they are. It works.

Training is where they can work on the stuff that doesn’t.

Go left. Lose it. Get coached. Try again.

That’s a big part of our Youth Camp: coaching, repetitions and plenty of live basketball.

It’s for players aged 11–15, and we’ve only got 30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

If your kid wants to get better, bring them down.
ads.headline: Kids use what works.
ads.creative_alt: A young player dribbles through a basketball skills exercise.

ads.primary_text:
If your kid can beat people going right, they’ll keep going right.

If they’re quicker than everyone, they’ll use their speed.

If one finish keeps working, they’ll keep using it.

Fair enough. They’re playing a game and trying to win.

But the stuff they can’t do yet needs somewhere to get worked on too.

Go left. Lose it.

Again.

Get the footwork wrong. Fix it.

Again.

Then put a defender there and see if it still works.

That’s what training gives young players that games sometimes don’t: time to work on the parts of their game that aren’t ready yet.

Our Youth Camp gives players aged 11–15 a full day of coaching, repetitions and live basketball.

There are 30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

If that sounds like a useful day for your kid, bring them down.
ads.headline: Kids use what works.
ads.creative_alt: A young player dribbles through a basketball skills exercise.

ads.primary_text:
If your kid has something that works in a game, they’re going to use it.

They should.

If they can beat their defender going right, go right.

If they’re quicker than everyone else, use the speed.

If they’ve got one finish they trust around the basket, that’s probably the finish they’re choosing when the score is close.

That’s basketball.

The problem is, games don’t always give young players much reason to work on what doesn’t work.

Nobody gets two minutes in the middle of a match to practise going left.

You don’t stop the game because their footwork was wrong.

And a player probably isn’t thinking, this would be an excellent time to try the move I’m terrible at.

Training gives them that space.

Go left.

Lose it.

Again.

Get coached.

Again.

Now get it right.

Good. Put a defender there.

That process isn’t as exciting as making three baskets in a game. But it’s where a lot of improvement happens.

That’s how we’re approaching our Youth Camp.

Players aged 11–15 will spend the day working on skills, decisions and competitive basketball with experienced coaches, including a former UCLA and NBA player.

We’ll work on things. We’ll play. We’ll stop and fix things. Then we’ll play again.

There are only 30 places because we want enough coaching time with the players who come.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

If your kid loves basketball and wants to get better at it, bring them down.

concepts.name: Confidence Comes After Doing It
concepts.strategy: Treat confidence as evidence earned through action rather than encouragement alone.
concepts.audience: Parents of players aged 11 to 15 who want their child to build grounded confidence through basketball.
concepts.proposition: Give players coached challenges and competitive moments that let them discover what they can do.

ads.primary_text:
Kids get confident when they realise they can actually do something.

Beat a defender they couldn’t beat before.

Use their left without losing the ball.

Play against someone good and hold their own.

You can tell a kid to believe in themselves all day.

Actually doing the thing works better.

That’s the kind of day we want to give them at our Youth Camp.

Ages 11–15. 30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Bring them down.
ads.headline: Confidence comes after doing it.
ads.creative_alt: A young basketball player rises to shoot during a camp session.

ads.primary_text:
You can tell a young player to be confident.

Sometimes they just need to do something that proves they can be.

Bring the ball up against pressure without panicking.

Make the pass they weren’t seeing before.

Play against someone better and realise they can compete.

Those little moments add up.

Because now confidence isn’t somebody saying, “Believe in yourself.”

It’s the player thinking, I know I can do that. I’ve done it.

That’s much more useful.

At our Youth Camp, players aged 11–15 get a full day to work on their game with experienced coaches, then test it in competitive basketball.

We’re keeping the camp to 30 players.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Give them a day to find a few more things they can do.
ads.headline: Confidence comes after doing it.
ads.creative_alt: A young basketball player rises to shoot during a camp session.

ads.primary_text:
Kids get confident when they realise they can actually do something.

Not when we tell them they’re amazing.

When they do it.

A player has been avoiding their left hand for months.

Then one day they use it, get past someone and finish.

Okay.

Now they know.

They normally panic when somebody pressures the ball.

This time they stay calm, protect it and get out.

Now they know that too.

Or they walk into a gym with players they’ve never met, feel a bit nervous, start playing and realise:

I’m alright here.

That’s confidence they’ve earned.

We sometimes get the order backwards with young players.

We want them to feel confident so they’ll try difficult things.

Quite often, trying difficult things is how they become confident.

So give them something they can’t quite do yet.

Help them with it.

Let them get it wrong.

Coach them.

Let them go again.

Then watch what happens when it starts working.

That’s the environment we want at our Youth Camp.

Players aged 11–15 will spend a full day working with experienced coaches — including a former UCLA and NBA player — through skills, decisions and live basketball.

We’re only taking 30 players.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

If your kid loves the game, bring them down and give them some things to figure out.

concepts.name: Getting Better Gets Harder To See
concepts.strategy: Describe how improvement becomes less obvious as players develop, shifting from new skills to better timing, decisions and positioning.
concepts.audience: Parents of developing players aged 11 to 15 whose progress now appears in smaller details.
concepts.proposition: Experienced coaches help players notice, understand and practise the details that make better basketball.

ads.primary_text:
When kids first start basketball, improvement is obvious.

They couldn’t dribble. Now they can.

Couldn’t make a layup. Now they can.

Later, getting better looks different.

Seeing the pass earlier. Using fewer dribbles. Knowing when not to drive.

Small things. Better basketball.

That’s the stuff we’ll be working on at our Youth Camp.

Ages 11–15. 30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.
ads.headline: Getting better gets harder to see.
ads.creative_alt: A School of Skill coach watches players closely during a basketball session.

ads.primary_text:
When a kid first starts basketball, you can almost watch them improve week by week.

First layup.

First proper jump shot.

They start using both hands.

Easy to see.

As they get better, the improvements get smaller.

They stop picking the ball up too early.

See a pass half a second quicker.

Change pace instead of just trying to run past everyone.

Make the simple play instead of the difficult one.

That stuff doesn’t always get a cheer from the sideline.

It’s still getting better.

At our Youth Camp, we’ll spend a full day working on those details — skills, decisions and then using them when the basketball becomes live.

For players aged 11–15.

30 places available.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Come and work on the little things.
ads.headline: Getting better gets harder to see.
ads.creative_alt: A School of Skill coach watches players closely during a basketball session.

ads.primary_text:
When kids first start basketball, getting better is pretty easy to spot.

They couldn’t dribble properly.

Now they can.

They couldn’t make a layup.

Now they can.

They learn to shoot, pass, change direction, use their other hand.

Big, obvious improvements.

Then they get better.

And weirdly, getting better becomes harder to see.

Now it might be taking one less dribble.

Seeing the help defender a little earlier.

Changing pace instead of just playing fast.

Knowing when to attack and when to move the ball.

Keeping their head up under pressure.

Getting into the right position before the ball even arrives.

Nobody in the stands is necessarily jumping up because your kid made the correct cut.

But it’s better basketball.

That’s where coaching starts becoming really useful.

Not just showing players another move.

Helping them notice more.

Understand more.

Make better choices.

Then giving them enough basketball to actually try it.

That’s what we’ll be doing at our Youth Camp with players aged 11–15.

A full day of skills, decisions, competition and coaching — including time with a former UCLA and NBA player.

We’re keeping it to 30 players so there’s actually time to coach them.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

If your kid is getting to the stage where the little things are starting to matter, bring them down.

concepts.name: Better Players Give You New Problems
concepts.strategy: Show why unfamiliar competition is useful: it stops familiar solutions and gives a young player a new basketball problem to solve.
concepts.audience: Parents of players aged 11 to 15 who need different competition to reveal the next part of their development.
concepts.proposition: Play against different players, discover what else your game needs and work on new answers with coaches.

ads.primary_text:
It’s easy to think a move is great when nobody can stop it.

Then you meet someone who can.

Good.

Now you need another answer.

That’s one of the useful things about playing different people. They show you parts of your game you don’t normally have to think about.

Our Youth Camp gives players aged 11–15 a full day to work, compete and figure some of that out.

30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Come and play.
ads.headline: Better players give you new problems.
ads.creative_alt: A young player shoots during a busy basketball camp session.

ads.primary_text:
Your kid might have a move that works every weekend.

Then they play someone quicker.

Doesn’t work.

They normally get wherever they want with the ball.

Now someone keeps them in front.

Good.

That’s useful.

Because now they have to find another way.

Change pace. Use the other hand. Move the ball. Try something else.

Playing different people shows young players things their normal basketball sometimes doesn’t.

And once you can see something, you can work on it.

That’s part of what our Youth Camp is for.

Players aged 11–15 will spend the day being coached, working on their skills and competing with other players.

We’ve got 30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Bring your game. Find out what else it needs.
ads.headline: Better players give you new problems.
ads.creative_alt: A young player shoots during a busy basketball camp session.

ads.primary_text:
A young player can get very comfortable with something that works.

Maybe they’re quicker than most of the kids they play.

Maybe they can get to the basket whenever they want.

Maybe there’s one move nobody at their club seems able to stop.

Great.

Then somebody stops it.

That’s useful.

Not because young players need somebody to “humble” them. That stuff gets silly.

It’s useful because now basketball is asking them a new question.

What else have you got?

Can you change pace?

Can you go the other way?

Can you give the ball up and get it back?

Can you still have a good game when your favourite thing isn’t working?

Players need those moments.

Otherwise it’s very easy to keep doing the same thing because it keeps working.

Different players give you different problems.

Different problems make you find different answers.

That’s why we want plenty of live basketball at our Youth Camp, not just drills.

Players aged 11–15 will get coached, work on their game and then test it against other players.

We’re keeping the camp to 30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Come and find a few new answers.
ads.headline: Better players give you new problems.
ads.creative_alt: A young player shoots during a busy basketball camp session.

concepts.name: Mistakes Give You Something To Coach
concepts.strategy: Normalise purposeful mistakes in training as useful information that lets a coach diagnose, correct and give the player another attempt.
concepts.audience: Parents of players aged 11 to 15 who want a serious but supportive learning environment.
concepts.proposition: Players try unfamiliar skills, receive specific feedback and test the correction again in live basketball.

ads.primary_text:
If a kid never loses the ball in training, they might not be trying anything new.

Go left. Lose it.

Fine.

Why did you lose it?

Fix that bit.

Go again.

A mistake you understand is useful.

That’s how we want players working at our Youth Camp — try things, get coached, try again, then put it into a game.

Ages 11–15. 30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.
ads.headline: Mistakes give you something to coach.
ads.creative_alt: A School of Skill coach demonstrates ball control during an individual drill.

ads.primary_text:
We don’t want young players scared of making mistakes in training.

If they’re learning something new, some of it is going to go wrong.

That’s normal.

Lose the ball.

Okay. Why?

Footwork?

Too high?

Wrong angle?

Fix it.

Again.

Now we’ve got something useful.

The point isn’t to celebrate every mistake. It’s to actually use them.

That’s what coaching is there for.

At our Youth Camp, players aged 11–15 get a full day to work on their game, get feedback and keep having another go.

Then we put it into live basketball and see what sticks.

Only 30 players are coming into the gym.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Bring them down.
ads.headline: Mistakes give you something to coach.
ads.creative_alt: A School of Skill coach demonstrates ball control during an individual drill.

ads.primary_text:
If your kid is learning something new in basketball, there’s a decent chance they’re going to be bad at it for a while.

That’s sort of how learning works.

Going left feels awkward.

The new footwork is slower than what they normally do.

They see the pass too late.

They try the move and lose the ball.

Fine.

Now there’s something to coach.

Why did it go wrong?

What did they miss?

What needs changing?

Try again.

The alternative is a player who only ever does the things they already know they can do.

They’ll probably make fewer mistakes.

They’ll also have a harder time adding anything new to their game.

Training should be one of the places where young players are allowed to get something wrong and actually learn from it.

Not careless.

Not messing about.

Just trying something that isn't comfortable yet.

That’s the environment we want at our Youth Camp.

Players aged 11–15 will get a full day of coaching, skill work and live basketball, with experienced coaches including a former UCLA and NBA player.

Try it.

Get some feedback.

Try it again.

Then see if you can do it when somebody’s defending you.

There are 30 places for the day.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

If your kid wants to work on their game, that’s exactly what we’ll be doing.

ads.creative_alt: A School of Skill coach demonstrates ball control during an individual drill.

concepts.name: What Do They Take Home?
concepts.strategy: Set an honest limit on what one camp can do, then define success as something useful the player understands and continues working on afterwards.
concepts.audience: Parents of players aged 11 to 15 who want practical value from a one-day basketball camp.
concepts.proposition: A full day designed to leave each player with useful corrections, ideas and motivation they can take back to training.

ads.primary_text:
A camp lasts one day.

The useful bit is what your kid still has afterwards.

Something they understand better.

Something they know they need to fix.

Something new to practise.

That’s a good day.

Our Youth Camp gives 30 players aged 11–15 a full day of coaching and basketball.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Come for the day.

Take something useful back to training.
ads.headline: What do they take home?
ads.creative_alt: A young basketball player sits courtside holding a ball and watching the gym.

ads.primary_text:
Nobody becomes a completely different basketball player in one day.

We’re not going to pretend they do.

But one day can give a young player something useful.

A coach spots something.

A correction finally clicks.

They learn a new way to solve a problem.

They play against someone different and realise what they need to work on.

Then they take that back to training.

That’s a good camp.

Our Youth Camp gives players aged 11–15 a full day of coaching, skill work and competitive basketball.

We’re taking 30 players.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

Hopefully they leave with something they’re still using after the camp is over.

Bring them down.
ads.headline: What do they take home?
ads.creative_alt: A young basketball player sits courtside holding a ball and watching the gym.

ads.primary_text:
A basketball camp lasts a day.

So there’s only so much we’re going to claim about it.

Your kid isn’t arriving in the morning as one player and leaving that afternoon completely transformed.

Come on.

But they can leave with something.

Maybe a coach notices why they keep struggling with a particular finish.

Maybe something they’ve heard ten times finally makes sense when somebody explains it differently.

Maybe they play against someone good and realise they can handle themselves.

Maybe they discover something in their game that needs more work.

Maybe they simply come home wanting to get outside with a ball and practise something they learned.

All of those are useful.

Because the important part of a camp isn’t only what happens while the player is there.

It’s what they take back with them.

That’s how we’re looking at our Youth Camp.

Players aged 11–15 get a full day of skill work, decision-making and competitive basketball with experienced coaches, including a former UCLA and NBA player.

We’ll give them plenty to do.

We’d rather they leave with a few things they actually remember.

There are 30 places.

Registration closes Wednesday 23 September.

If your kid loves basketball, bring them down. We’ll give them something to work on.
